hiringAttributes.title: General Cognitive Ability (GCA)
hiringAttributes.description: How you reason through an unfamiliar problem: structure, assumptions, and adaptation when the constraints move. Interviewers score the path, not only the destination.
hiringAttributes.howItShowsUp: Embedded in coding and design rounds — clarifying questions, trade-off reasoning, and how you recover when your first idea fails.

hiringAttributes.title: Role-Related Knowledge (RRK)
hiringAttributes.description: Actual engineering depth: data structures, algorithms, language fluency, testing instinct, and — from L5 — system architecture judgement.
hiringAttributes.howItShowsUp: Coding rounds and, where applicable, the systems round. Your language should be one you can write fluently without an IDE.

hiringAttributes.title: Leadership (emergent)
hiringAttributes.description: Stepping up when your skills fit the problem and stepping back when they do not. Assessed for individual contributors too, not just managers.
hiringAttributes.howItShowsUp: Behavioural round; also in how you handle disagreement with the interviewer about an approach.

hiringAttributes.title: Googleyness
hiringAttributes.description: Comfort with ambiguity, bias to action, intellectual humility, collaboration, and doing the right thing for users.
hiringAttributes.howItShowsUp: The Googleyness & Leadership round, via STAR-L stories, and in your tone across every round.

stages.name: Application and resume screen
stages.focus: Recruiter or automated screen against the posting's qualifications.
tips: Lead each bullet with impact and a number, not with the technology list.
Name the language you want to be interviewed in and keep it consistent across the resume.
A referral moves the screen along faster than a cover letter does.
Apply to a small number of well-matched postings rather than many at once.

stages.name: Google Hiring Assessment (GHA)
stages.focus: Non-technical work-style and situational-judgement questionnaire sent by the recruiter before or just after the screen.
tips: Not a coding test — it asks how you work, prioritise, and handle ambiguity.
Answer consistently rather than strategically; contradictory answers are the visible failure mode.
Complete it promptly; the loop usually does not advance until it is in.
Some new-grad and intern pipelines add a separate timed coding assessment — confirm with your recruiter which applies to you.

stages.name: Recruiter screen
stages.focus: Background, timeline, target level, and process overview.
tips: Prepare a 90-second pitch aligned to Google-scale problems.
Ask directly which rounds your loop contains — the format varies by region, level and team, and is changing in 2026.
Ask whether a systems round is in your loop and whether the code-comprehension pilot applies.
Confirm the level being targeted; it determines whether design is scored at all.

stages.name: Technical phone screen
stages.focus: One or two coding questions in a shared editor with no autocomplete.
tips: Clarify inputs, constraints, and edge cases before writing code.
Propose brute force, then optimise; state time and space complexity out loud.
Write compiling, testable code and dry-run a small example.
Expect medium arrays/hashing/strings or a graph traversal; hard-only screens are rare.

stages.name: Onsite / virtual onsite loop
stages.focus: L3/L4: 3–4 coding rounds plus one Googleyness & Leadership round. L5+: a dedicated systems design round replaces a coding round.
tips: Treat each round independently — a weak round does not have to spread.
At L4 a systems round is often optional or substituted for a coding round; ask rather than assume.
Design scoring starts in earnest at L5; at L4 design usually surfaces inside a coding round as a follow-up.
Googleyness: STAR-L stories showing ambiguity, collaboration, user focus, and a real mistake.
Leave 3–5 minutes for follow-ups — they often decide the marginal hire/no-hire.

stages.name: Code comprehension round (2026 pilot)
stages.focus: Read, debug, and improve a 200–500 line codebase you did not write, in CoderPad, with Gemini available as an assistant.
tips: Piloted from May 2026 for junior and mid-level SWE roles on select US teams — confirm whether your loop includes it.
Scored on three things: prompt quality, validation of the model's output, and your own debugging reasoning.
Never accept a generated answer without stating how you verified it; unverified acceptance is the failure mode.
Practise reading unfamiliar code aloud: entry points, data flow, invariants, then the suspicious edges.
The classic algorithm rounds remain AI-free — do not assume assistance is allowed elsewhere.

stages.name: Hiring committee and team matching
stages.focus: Packet review by a committee that never met you, level calibration, then conversations with teams that have headcount.
tips: The committee reads interviewer notes, so clearly verbalised reasoning is what survives into the packet.
Consistent signals across rounds matter more than one spectacular round.
Level is argued from the scope of your past work plus interview depth; prepare a scope narrative.
Compare teams on product impact and growth, and ask about on-call and roadmap ownership.

codingTips: Start with examples and invariants; Google interviewers reward structured thinking over fast typing.
Name the pattern out loud (BFS, binary search on answer, interval greedy) — it earns partial credit when time runs short.
For graphs, state the representation (adjacency list vs matrix) and why before implementing.
When stuck, reduce the problem — smaller input, dropped constraint — then bridge back.
Always propose tests: empty input, single element, duplicates, maximum constraints.
Prefer readable names; no autocomplete means clarity beats cleverness.
If you optimise mid-round, say what changed in the complexity and why it is still correct.
Ask before assuming library help; then write the part being tested by hand.

roundPlaybooks.title: Coding round (45 min)
roundPlaybooks.timebox: 5 clarify · 5 approach · 20 code · 10 test and follow-ups
steps: Restate the problem and confirm input ranges, duplicates, and output shape.
State a brute force with complexity, then the target complexity.
Name the pattern, sketch the invariant, then write code top-down.
Dry-run one small and one degenerate case; fix in place, out loud.
Answer the follow-up as a design change, not a rewrite.

roundPlaybooks.title: Code comprehension round (60 min, 2026 pilot)
roundPlaybooks.timebox: 10 orient · 20 trace and hypothesise · 20 fix and verify · 10 improve
steps: Orient before reading line by line: entry points, module boundaries, data flow, tests.
Say your hypothesis before you prompt the assistant, so your reasoning is on record.
Use the assistant for breadth (where is X handled) and verify every claim against the code.
Fix the bug, then state how you would prove the fix — test, assertion, or log.
Close with one design-level improvement and its risk.

roundPlaybooks.title: Systems design round (45 min, L5+ or optional at L4)
roundPlaybooks.timebox: 8 requirements · 5 estimates · 12 high level · 15 deep dive · 5 wrap
steps: Separate functional requirements from NFRs (scale, latency, consistency, availability).
Do back-of-envelope numbers before drawing anything.
Draw the happy path end to end, then name the bottleneck.
Take one deep dive the interviewer cares about; state the trade-off you accept.
Close with failure modes and what you would monitor.

roundPlaybooks.title: Googleyness & Leadership round (45 min)
steps: Use STAR-L: situation, task, action, result, and the learning you carried forward.
Own the 'I' in the action; say what the team did separately from what you did.
Bring one genuine failure with a concrete change that followed.
In the 2026 pilot this round can include a technical deep dive on a past project — know your own architecture and its trade-offs.
End each story with the measurable outcome, then stop talking.

eligibility.l3: Typically 0–2 years relevant experience (new grad or early career). Coding fundamentals, learning velocity, and collaboration signals dominate; no system design round.
eligibility.l4: Typically ~2–5 years. Strong independent delivery and medium/hard coding. A systems round is often optional or substituted for a coding round — design is not usually the deciding signal.
eligibility.l5plus: Senior and above. A dedicated systems design round is standard, scope and cross-team influence dominate, and coding stays rigorous.
officialQuals: Bachelor's degree in CS or a related field, or equivalent practical experience — wording varies by posting.
Proficiency in one mainstream language; C++, Java, Python, Go and JavaScript are all accepted for interviews.
Demonstrated data structures, algorithms, and software engineering experience.
Ability to discuss technical work clearly in English.

verifyWithRecruiter: Which rounds are in my loop, and how many are coding?
Is a systems design round included at my target level?
Does the code comprehension pilot apply to this team?
Is the Google Hiring Assessment required before scheduling?
Which language do you recommend I interview in for this team?
disclaimer: Google's process and rubrics vary by region, level, team and year, and the 2026 code-comprehension round is a limited pilot. This file is study guidance compiled from Google's public careers pages and candidate reports on 2026-09-28 — not an official Google document. Confirm your loop's format with your recruiter.
